<reason>Both sides argued at a high level, but CON kept the debate anchored to the motion's "even when" clause and exposed that PRO's strongest evidence (German, French, Alpine, Scandinavian wolves) was natural recolonisation rather than deliberate release over objection. PRO's "crates versus paws" reply was memorable but CON's "authorship" answer and the Switzerland concession ("illegal killing for decades," "top up when losses occur") turned PRO's own design into evidence of an unsustainable pipeline. CON also answered both pressure questions directly with a defined consenting unit and an outcome-verified culling alternative, whereas PRO prematurely claimed CON's "silence" before CON's answer turn had occurred. PRO landed real damage with the "consent returns no by construction" and "locked door with the key inside" attacks, and CON's sequencing proposal is vulnerable to releasing where least needed. But PRO never addressed CON's point that lynx (ambush roe-deer predators) don't move red deer on the open hill—the core Scottish regeneration mechanism—nor the loss of species-rich grazed hillsides. Those drops plus the fit-to-motion problem give CON a clear but competitive win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2.1–B2.3: CON's reframing that every success on PRO's map "walked in" and that a consent rule doesn't strip funding from farmers facing naturally arriving wolves dissolved PRO's strongest counter (A2.5) and set up the "government's animal is the one that gets shot" line that carried through to the closing.</best_rebuttal>
